title: What animal do you see?
caption: Which parts of the photograph helped you decide?
notes:
What animal is this, and which parts made you decide?
Point to the face, fur, and silhouette before mentioning an architecture.

title: Find the dog photos in a folder
caption: Each photograph gets one label. Decide what the labels mean before choosing the model.
notes:
What would you want the program to return for each photo?
Reveal dog and cat. Connect one image label to the spam/not-spam example in Part I.

title: What were we asking the text model to predict?
caption: A prefix supplies the context. The answer is a distribution over the next token.
notes:
After predicting one letter, how would we generate a whole name?
Follow the loop back to the input, now with one more token.

title: What are we asking the image model to predict?
caption: We observe the whole photograph and predict one label for it.
notes:
Are we trying to guess a missing patch in this task?
Point to the full observed image and the two possible class labels.

title: What changed, and what stayed the same?
caption: Both models score possible answers. What they observe, summarize and predict differs.
notes:
Which parts of our old calculation can we reuse unchanged?
Compare one row at a time. Refer to the image summary from the preceding slide; its construction comes later.

title: Suppose we also want to crop out the animal
caption: A class label tells us what is present. A box also tells us where to look.
notes:
Is the word dog enough for an automatic crop?
Reveal the illustrative box and ask which extra numbers describe it.

title: Find the photo that matches this description
caption: Here we need to compare an image with words.
notes:
Which of our two photographs fits the first description?
Match the words to visible evidence, then connect this task to the later CLIP lesson.

title: Would you recognize this crop on its own?
caption: A dark crop may be fur, shadow or background. The full photo gives us clues.
notes:
Could this dark crop be fur, a shadow, or something else?
Reveal where it came from; keep pointing to the same crop.

title: What can we carry over from our text models?
caption: We still turn inputs into rows, read useful information, and predict an answer.
notes:
What stays the same when the input is a photograph?
Point to representation, contextual reading, and multiple head messages in the earlier examples.

title: Is this dark region fur or background?
caption: Face clues could make a dark crop easier to interpret. The final prediction is one label for the whole image.
notes:
Does this dark crop alone tell us whether the photograph contains a dog or a cat?
Reveal the eye and face crops. Ask what they add, then return to the whole-image classification task.

title: Can a CNN use the rest of the image too?
caption: Stacking local filters lets a CNN use a wider view. Attention gives rows another way to exchange information.
notes:
Does attention have a monopoly on context?
Point to a local neighbourhood; describe how stacked convolutions widen the receptive field.

title: Where do the patch boundaries go?
caption: The grid cuts through the photograph before the model knows where the dog is.
notes:
Does each patch contain one whole object?
Reveal the grid, then match each enlarged crop back to its location.

title: How can a red pixel be three numbers?
caption: Each pixel records a red, green and blue channel.
notes:
What would [0,0,0] look like?
Name the channels, then ask for black, red and white before revealing the rows.

title: How many numbers are in four RGB pixels?
caption: Four pixels, three channels each: twelve numbers.
notes:
Does one pixel contribute one number or three?
Count RGB channels before flattening.

title: Write those twelve numbers in one row
caption: Keep the same pixel order each time.
notes:
Which three entries came from the white pixel?
Trace each RGB triple back to its coloured pixel.

title: Which pixel goes first in the row?
caption: Choose an order and use it for every patch.
notes:
Where does the last 1 in this row come from?
Trace the four pixel positions in raster order.

title: Give each patch its own row of pixels
caption: A row starts with the pixel values from one fixed part of the image.
notes:
Do we mix pixels from different patches at this step?
Follow one crop into its own row.

title: Use the same projection on every patch
caption: Every output row has the same width, so the attention block can process them together.
notes:
How many different projection matrices do we need?
Point to the shared operation between the four rows.

title: How many weights turn pixels into a patch row?
caption: One learned projection is shared across locations. Positions enter afterwards.
notes:
Does doubling the number of patches double the projection parameters?
Trace one row through the matrix and bias; then reuse that operation for all patches.

title: Same pieces, different picture?
caption: Count the filled patches in each image. Then look at where they are.
notes:
How many filled and empty patches are in each image?
Reveal the second arrangement. Count two of each, then ask what changed.

title: Could you put the picture back together?
caption: Knowing which patches we have does not tell us where each one belongs.
notes:
What information was discarded when we made this bag?
Ask students to reconstruct the original layout; reveal that both layouts fit.

title: Flatten P1 so we can multiply it
caption: These are the same four pixel values, in a fixed order.
notes:
Where does each entry in the row come from?
Point to one pixel and its matching row entry.

title: Compute the first coordinate of P1
caption: This chosen column takes the mean of the four pixels.
notes:
What is one quarter of each pixel, added together?
Add all four terms before revealing 1.

title: Write the whole content row
caption: The first coordinate is ink; the final 1 comes from the bias.
notes:
What happened to the two middle coordinates?
Use the zero columns and then add the bias.

title: Where does each number in the patch row come from?
caption: Multiply the pixel row by each column, then add the bias.
notes:
Which column computes ink, and which columns are zero?
Calculate all four coordinates, then add the bias.

title: What row does an empty patch get?
caption: The bias adds a learned offset even when every input pixel is zero.
notes:
Will multiplying zeros by W_patch produce the final 1?
Calculate the product first, then add the bias as a separate step.

title: Would the mean pixel value tell these patches apart?
caption: A patch can have the same average and a different pattern.
notes:
Which patch has a horizontal edge? Which has a vertical edge?
Count two ones in each, then compare their positions.

title: Could two projection columns keep that difference?
caption: Each column combines the same pixels in a different way.
notes:
What does the first column subtract from what?
Calculate the top-edge patch against each column, then try the left-edge patch.

title: We have several patch rows. Where does the answer go?
caption: The classification token (CLS) is an extra learned row used to collect information for the image label.
notes:
We have many contextual patch rows. How could we produce one image label?
Point to the extra row and spell out classification token. It gathers information before the classifier produces a label.

title: Where does CLS come from?
caption: CLS is an extra learned input vector with the same width as a patch row.
notes:
Which image pixels were used to create CLS?
Point to the separate parameter, then count five rows entering attention.

title: How can the same starting CLS describe different pictures?
caption: Its starting vector is shared. The keys and values it reads come from the current image.
notes:
Does a shared first-layer query force the output to be identical?
Follow each image through its own source keys, values and weighted sum.

title: These patches look the same. How do we tell them apart?
caption: Their content rows match. Their positions do not.
notes:
Which coordinate changes for the top-right patch?
Keep the filled patch content fixed and add its column location.

title: Give each patch a location vector
caption: Two patches can look alike and still come from different places.
notes:
Which entries record the row and column here?
Read each location from the small image grid.

title: Add content and location, coordinate by coordinate
caption: These five rows form E, the input to our attention calculation.
notes:
What distinguishes P1 from P2 now?
Compare the two filled patches after adding positions.

title: Can the top-left patch read the bottom-right?
caption: We already have the whole image when we predict its label, so all patches can read one another.
notes:
What future information would leak from another patch in this task?
Compare a lower-triangular next-token mask with all-to-all image attention.

title: Why did our text predictor hide later tokens?
caption: A causal mask prevents the model from reading the answer it is meant to predict.
notes:
Would seeing the next training token make prediction unfairly easy?
Read one matrix row as a receiver and its permitted source columns.

title: Why do we make three versions of each row?
caption: Matching a source and reading its information are two different jobs.
notes:
Which two vectors decide the weight, and which vector gets multiplied by it?
Recall bank’s request and river’s information from Part II. Keep the photo crop visible.

title: Which part of the picture could help this dark crop?
caption: Imagine borrowing nearby face evidence to interpret a patch of dark fur.
notes:
Would the face crop or the branches help more with this particular ambiguity?
Keep the receiver fixed and point to two possible sources.

title: Each row makes a query, a key and a value
caption: Q and K decide the weights. V supplies the message that gets weighted.
notes:
Can the same patch receive information and also send information?
Trace all three projections from the same row.

title: How could the face crop get more weight?
caption: Exponentiate the two scores: 3 and 1. Their shares are ¾ and ¼.
notes:
Where does the factor 3 come from?
Multiply q by each key, then normalize the two exponentials.

title: What do we receive after choosing those weights?
caption: Multiply each source’s value by its weight, then add the two vectors.
notes:
Does choosing the face with ¾ weight discard the other source?
Calculate both contributions before adding them.

title: Change only the keys. What happens?
caption: The values stay available, but their shares in the message change.
notes:
Which source now gets three times the weight of the other?
Swap the two keys and recompute the mixture.

title: Change only a value. What happens?
caption: The attention weights stay the same, but the received information changes.
notes:
Would an attention heatmap show this change?
Keep the two weights visible while doubling the first value coordinate.

title: Do we type a question into this classifier?
caption: No text prompt is needed. The image rows generate their own Q, K and V.
notes:
Where does the query come from if nobody types a question?
Follow the numerical projection from the input rows.

title: Which weights create the query, key and value?
caption: One input row; three separate learned projections. These worksheet weights are chosen for arithmetic.
notes:
What does each nonzero matrix entry copy or scale?
Follow the constant into Q, then ink and row into K and V.

title: Where does the CLS query [1,1] come from?
caption: Each query coordinate is a dot product with one column of W_Q.
notes:
Which input coordinate supplies both ones?
Use the W_Q columns shown on the previous slide and multiply all four terms.

title: How does P1 get the key [√2,0]?
caption: Head 1 keeps ink and row in its keys.
notes:
Would the constant 1 in the input affect this key?
Point to the zero in the last row of each key column.

title: Which features does this head compare?
caption: Part II again: the query and keys choose where to read.
notes:
What does multiplying this input by W_Q do?
Point to the fixed last coordinate supplying [1,1]. Then construct P1’s key.

title: Can we work out one score before filling the table?
caption: The head has two query/key coordinates, so d_k is 2.
notes:
Should the denominator use 2, 4 or 5 here?
Distinguish head width, embedding width and number of source rows.

title: What does softmax do when the scores tie?
caption: Equal scores get equal shares. Only score differences affect the shares.
notes:
Are two very negative scores less than 100% in total?
Compare the first and third rows, then explain the middle row using exponentials 1 and 3.

title: Repeat the dot product for every source
caption: Keep the query fixed. Only the source key changes.
notes:
Which of these keys give the same score?
Work down the five sources, including CLS.

title: Exponentiate the five scores
caption: Scores 0 and 1 become 1 and e.
notes:
Why are four exponentials equal?
Match each exponential to its score.

title: Divide by one shared sum
caption: The five source weights now add up to one.
notes:
What fraction belongs to CLS?
Divide its exponential 1 by the same sum used for every patch.

title: Where does the 0.229 beside P1 come from?
caption: Every source appears in the same denominator, including CLS.
notes:
What would go wrong if each patch used a different denominator?
Sum the five source contributions first, then divide one exponential by that sum.

title: Put each value beside its weight
caption: Keep a patch’s weight and value on the same row.
notes:
Which value belongs to the weight for P3?
Trace the source label across the table.

title: Multiply the value by its weight
caption: One scalar scales both coordinates of the source value.
notes:
Does the second coordinate get a different weight?
Multiply both entries before moving to the next row.

title: Add the contributions to get one message
caption: Add down each coordinate column.
notes:
How do five source rows become a two-number message?
Sum each coordinate separately, then reveal the result.

title: Can an empty patch still send something?
caption: An empty patch still has a position, and its value can carry that information.
notes:
Which coordinate receives the contribution from P3?
Multiply both coordinates by the same weight; keep the zero visible.

title: Do equal weights send equal information?
caption: Compare the values beside the weights. They tell us what each patch sends.
notes:
What do these two patches contribute to the ink coordinate?
Multiply both coordinates and compare the resulting messages.

title: What if the query cared only about ink?
caption: Change the query and keep the sources fixed. The mixture changes.
notes:
Which filled patches should get more weight now?
Set the second query coordinate to zero, then recompute all five scores.

title: Would a second way of reading the image help?
caption: As with colour and material in the coat example, we can keep two different messages.
notes:
What two kinds of information might help distinguish these layouts?
Point to row and column. Keep the same patches on both sides.

title: Head 2 compares ink and column
caption: The same input rows now pass through a different key projection.
notes:
Which patch has both ink and column equal to 1?
Point to P2 before calculating its score.

title: Give Head 2 its own softmax
caption: Each head divides by its own sum of exponentials.
notes:
Can we reuse Head 1’s denominator here?
Compare the score lists before normalizing.

title: What information does Head 2 send?
caption: Its values carry ink and column.
notes:
Which value coordinate changed from Head 1?
Keep the same source labels while comparing value definitions.

title: Calculate each Head 2 contribution
caption: Use Head 2’s weight and Head 2’s value from the same source.
notes:
Which source contributes most to the ink coordinate?
Compute P2’s product, then compare the other sources.

title: Add Head 2’s contributions
caption: We now have a second two-number message.
notes:
Are the two heads’ messages equal?
Compare the sums with Head 1’s result.

title: Do the patch rows get updated too?
caption: Yes. Here every query is [1,1], so the messages match. Each row still has its own starting vector.
notes:
Do identical messages imply identical updated rows?
Compare the queries, then remind students that each residual starts from a different E row.

title: Keep both messages by putting them side by side
caption: Concatenation gives us four numbers; it does not average the heads.
notes:
What would we lose by averaging these two rows immediately?
Follow all four coordinates into the joined row.

title: Use W_O to make the first update coordinate
caption: The first column subtracts Head 2’s ink value from Head 1’s.
notes:
Which two entries of W_O make that subtraction?
Trace the +1 and −1 from the joined row.

title: Collect all four output coordinates
caption: The update has the same width as the row we will add it to.
notes:
Why do we need four update coordinates?
Match the update width to E before moving to the residual.

title: What do the other columns of W_O produce?
caption: Use the same joined row for every output coordinate.
notes:
Which column adds information from both heads?
Read W_O column by column, matching these results to the full update vector.

title: What if attention sent a zero message?
caption: The residual gives the next block a direct path from the starting row.
notes:
Would the original row disappear if the attention output were zero?
Add coordinate by coordinate, then connect this to the nonzero update in our main example.

title: Add the message to the starting CLS row
caption: Only the last starting coordinate is nonzero in this example.
notes:
Which coordinate changes because the original CLS contains a 1?
Add the two rows one coordinate at a time.

title: Use the updated CLS row to score the two labels
caption: The class matrix maps four coordinates to two scores.
notes:
Why does a negative first coordinate favour Across here?
Apply −4 and +4 to that same coordinate.

title: We used softmax twice. What changed?
caption: The formula is the same. The alternatives being compared are different.
notes:
Should the five attention weights sum with the two class probabilities?
Circle the alternatives separately. Each softmax has its own denominator.

title: Turn the class scores into probabilities
caption: The alternatives here are Across and Down.
notes:
Which two exponentials belong in this denominator?
Normalize over the two labels, then read the bars.

title: Use the known label to calculate the loss
caption: For this image, the correct label is Across the top.
notes:
Which probability belongs inside the logarithm?
Keep the image and correct label visible while calculating the loss.

title: How much does a confident wrong answer cost?
caption: Training lowers the loss by increasing the probability of the known label.
notes:
Which prediction should receive the largest penalty?
Compare all three cases using the same correct label.

title: Use the gradient to change the class bias
caption: Subtract half the gradient from the two bias values.
notes:
Why does the correct class bias increase?
Read the sign of p minus the one-hot target.

title: Run the prediction again after that update
caption: The correct-class probability rises and its loss falls on this example.
notes:
Did changing the bias alter the image or the attention weights?
Keep the frozen worksheet separate from the two bias values we changed.

title: Move the patches. Does the answer change?
caption: Make a prediction, change the arrangement, then turn positions off.
notes:
Will the class probabilities change if we permute patches without position information?
Take a prediction, choose Down the left, then turn positions off.

title: Who teaches CLS what information to collect?
caption: The image-classification loss sends gradients through the classifier and the attention blocks.
notes:
Is there a separate label telling CLS which patch to read?
Trace the loss backward through the computational path.

title: Could we classify the image without CLS?
caption: Averaging the final patch rows gives one image summary. This is called mean pooling.
notes:
Can you calculate the two coordinates of the mean?
Add each column and divide by the number of patch rows.

title: So why use CLS in our ViT?
caption: It gives the model a dedicated row whose final representation is trained for the image label.
notes:
What must both of these paths produce before the class head?
Follow each route to one fixed-width vector.

title: Put the familiar attention inside a full block
caption: Attention mixes information across rows. The MLP transforms each row separately.
notes:
Which operation communicates between patches, and which works on one row at a time?
Point to attention, then the MLP; trace both residual paths.

title: Which operation lets one patch borrow from another?
caption: Attention mixes source value rows using weights chosen for the receiver.
notes:
Which arrows cross from one patch to another?
Point to several source rows contributing to one destination row.

title: What does the MLP change?
caption: The MLP combines coordinates within each row and applies a nonlinearity.
notes:
Does this MLP directly read a neighbouring patch row?
Keep one row highlighted as it passes through the two linear layers.

title: What average are we subtracting?
caption: LayerNorm works across the coordinates of this one row.
notes:
Are the other patches included in this mean?
Keep the four coordinates together and calculate their mean.

title: How spread out is the centered row?
caption: Square the deviations, take their mean, then take the square root.
notes:
Why do positive and negative deviations not cancel here?
Square each deviation before averaging. Mention epsilon on the next slide.

title: What does LayerNorm do to one row?
caption: Normalize across the coordinates of each token, independently of other tokens.
notes:
Which numbers participate in the mean and variance?
Use the four coordinates of one row; do not average across patches or the batch.

title: How does the MLP make a wider row?
caption: The first linear layer mixes coordinates within the same token.
notes:
Where does the zero in the hidden row come from?
Compute 1×1 + (−1)×1 using the third column.

title: Apply GELU to each hidden coordinate
caption: GELU(1) is about 0.841, and GELU(−1) is about −0.159.
notes:
Does GELU send every negative input to zero?
Compare the two signs using these actual values.

title: How does the MLP return to the original width?
caption: The second linear layer produces an update that can be added to the starting row.
notes:
Why must the output width be two in this example?
Match its width to the residual row [1,−1].

title: Add the MLP message to the starting row
caption: Both vectors have width two, so we can add them coordinate by coordinate.
notes:
Where does the 1.841 come from?
Add 1 and 0.841, then repeat for the second coordinate.

title: What does the next block get to see?
caption: The next block starts from rows that have already read the image.
notes:
Has the query in block two already seen other patches indirectly?
Trace the first residual update into the next block’s query projection.

title: How many rows does the real photograph produce?
caption: A 14-by-14 patch grid gives 196 patch rows, plus CLS.
notes:
Why is there one more row than image patches?
Count the grid, then add the summary row.

title: How many blocks process those rows?
caption: This checkpoint has 12 blocks and three heads in each block.
notes:
Does every head read the same input rows?
Recall the shared E and separate projections from our two-head calculation.

title: What changed when we made the model larger?
caption: There are more patches, wider rows and more blocks. The operations follow the same pattern.
notes:
Which dimensions are different from our four-patch worksheet?
Trace pixels, patch rows, blocks and the 1,000 class scores.

title: These two 16s mean different things
caption: Patch count comes from the image grid. Row width is a model choice.
notes:
Which 16 changes if we use a larger image with the same patch size?
Point to the row axis, then to the coordinate axis.

title: How do image pixels become rows in code?
caption: A non-overlapping convolution implements the shared patch projection.
notes:
Why does this convolution produce exactly one output per patch?
Follow kernel size 2 and stride 2 across an 8×8 image.

title: Why does our ViT code use Conv2d?
caption: One filter computes the same dot product as one column of the patch-projection matrix.
notes:
Have we already calculated this number using a flattened patch?
Match the four pixel–weight pairs to the top-minus-bottom column in our earlier edge example.

title: How far should the filter move?
caption: A stride equal to the patch width gives non-overlapping patches.
notes:
What would happen if the stride were one?
Move the 2×2 outline two columns, then two rows; keep the weights unchanged.

title: Does this layer merely cut up the image?
caption: Conv2d both selects each patch and applies a learned linear projection.
notes:
Where are the trainable numbers in this operation?
Count four weights and one bias per filter, then read each output as a two-coordinate row.

title: Can you match each line to our calculation?
caption: Each row of A sums to one across its sources. Multiplying by V adds the weighted messages.
notes:
Which axis must sum to one?
Match the source dimension in A to the row dimension in V.

title: Can a patch in image A read image B?
caption: Ordinary image self-attention gives each image its own source rows.
notes:
Should putting a second photograph in the batch change the first image’s message?
Keep the two groups of rows separate; identify the image, token and coordinate axes.

title: A tensor can have the right shape and the wrong meaning
caption: Set Q=K=0, V=X and W_O=I. Each output is an average. With [B,N,D] input, batch_first=True keeps that average within each image.
notes:
Which axis should softmax normalize over in each image?
Use uniform attention to calculate the first output row under both interpretations.

title: A quick check before training
caption: Run the same image alone and beside another image. Its attention output should agree.
notes:
Why does the wrong version change when B is added?
Compare the first patch’s output under both layouts before looking at any accuracy curve.

title: What is the complete pre-LayerNorm block?
caption: MultiheadAttention includes concatenation and W_O. Both residual additions keep width D.
notes:
Where did the output projection go in this code?
Open the accompanying Block class: PyTorch’s attention module owns out_proj.

title: How do we add one CLS row per image?
caption: Every image starts with the same learned CLS vector.
notes:
Do we need a separate learned CLS parameter for each training image?
Expand the same parameter across the batch, then concatenate along the row axis.

title: Where does location enter the code?
caption: Broadcast the same position table across the batch.
notes:
Which position vector goes with the third image patch?
Point to CLS at index 0 and patch P3 at index 3.

title: Which row reaches the classifier?
caption: We keep all rows through the blocks, then select CLS for this image-label task.
notes:
Why is the second index zero here?
Point to the row dimension; the batch dimension stays in place.

title: How does the full model produce image logits?
caption: Only the final readout selects CLS. Every transformer block processes all rows.
notes:
At what point do we discard the patch rows for classification?
Keep all 17 rows through both blocks, then select x[:,0].

title: Which call makes this model learn?
caption: Pass raw logits to cross_entropy. It combines log-softmax with the label loss.
notes:
Which line computes gradients, and which one changes the weights?
Distinguish backward from step. Point back to Part I’s learning loop.

title: When are gradients computed?
caption: backward computes gradients. The parameter values stay where they are until the optimizer step.
notes:
Would another forward pass already use new weights?
Separate computing a derivative from using it to change a parameter.

title: Which line changes the weights?
caption: The optimizer uses the gradients to update the parameters.
notes:
Are AdamW updates exactly minus learning-rate times gradient?
Recall the simple SGD bias example, then distinguish the optimizer used in this lab.

title: Will the model recognize a new noisy stripe?
caption: Move the stripe and vary the pixel values. Keep separate images for training, validation and testing.
notes:
What would memorizing our original two clean images fail to demonstrate?
Compare noisy samples, then identify the roles of the three splits.

title: Which images are allowed to influence the weights?
caption: Give each split one job before starting the experiment.
notes:
Why should we not keep trying checkpoints on the test set?
Follow the three arrows in order. Validation chooses the checkpoint; test reports its result.

title: Suppose the model gets this training image wrong
caption: The loss uses the probability of the known label, even when the model prefers the other one.
notes:
Which of the two probabilities belongs inside the logarithm?
Keep the label horizontal visible while students choose the correct probability.

title: What does one epoch mean in this experiment?
caption: An epoch visits every training example once.
notes:
How many weight updates happen during one pass through the training set?
Divide 512 by 64; then distinguish an epoch from an optimizer step.

title: Is the model improving on its training images?
caption: Training accuracy measures the examples used for the weight updates.
notes:
Could memorization alone make this curve look good?
Read the training curve before revealing validation.

title: Does the improvement carry over to validation?
caption: Validation images help us choose a checkpoint without using the test set.
notes:
What would a widening gap between the curves suggest?
Compare the curves at the same epoch.

title: Can training make up for missing positions?
caption: Train on the same images with the same recipe, then compare the two test results.
notes:
Can any amount of training recover layout from the patch bag in this setup?
Reveal both test counts; connect the 50% result to paired permutation invariance.

title: Which pixels are we giving the real model?
caption: The model receives the square crop on the right, after RGB normalization.
notes:
Are we feeding the original rectangular photograph directly to the network?
Match the original to the evaluation crop, then mention normalization.

title: What did the model call our dog?
caption: These probabilities come from running this photograph through the pretrained model.
notes:
What answer should the model assign to our opening image?
Reveal the saved top-three predictions. Compare the model’s label with the students’ original answer.

title: Does one correct photograph tell us the accuracy?
caption: To estimate accuracy, count correct predictions over an appropriate test set.
notes:
Can we report 95.7% accuracy from a 95.7% probability on one dog?
Separate a model’s probability on one image from a fraction correct over many images.

title: What happens when we give it the cat?
caption: Keep the same model and preprocessing. Change only the photograph.
notes:
Do we change model weights when a different test image arrives?
Reveal the top three ImageNet labels and probabilities.

title: Where did the checkpoint learn its visual features?
caption: Pretraining uses many images to fit a starting model.
notes:
Are we starting the photo experiment with random weights?
Point to the pretraining phase and the supplied checkpoint.

title: How would we adapt it to our own labels?
caption: Fit a new classifier; choose whether to update the image encoder too.
notes:
What changes if our labels are only cat and dog?
Distinguish a frozen-encoder linear probe from fine-tuning.

title: What happens when we classify a new photograph?
caption: Inference uses the fitted weights without updating them.
notes:
Does the model train again for every new photo?
Follow a new image through the fixed network.

title: What is one coloured square actually showing?

title: Do the heads read the same places?
caption: Block 12, CLS query, heads 1–3. The colour scale is the same in all three images.
notes:
Which similarities and differences can you see across heads?
Read the 14×14 source grid and the separately reported CLS self-weight.

title: Does CLS read differently in a later block?
caption: Compare the first and last blocks on the same image and colour scale.
notes:
What changed between the two query representations?

title: What does this particular patch read?
caption: The purple square is the receiver. The shading shows its source weights in block 12, head 1.
notes:
Which row of the attention matrix did we select this time?

title: What changes when the patch size is halved?
caption: At fixed image size, half the patch width gives four times as many patch rows.
notes:
Will attention-score count grow by four or roughly sixteen?
Count rows first, then square the total including CLS.

title: How much matching happens inside the tiny real model?
caption: Even this small ViT compares many pairs of rows.
notes:
How can a 14-by-14 patch grid produce more than a million scores?
Count pairs, then heads, then blocks. Keep token count separate from pixel count.

title: What happens if we use a larger image?
caption: Work out the token count before you change the controls.
notes:
What happens to the 197-token sequence at resolution 384?
Ask for a count, change the control, and compare with the prediction.

title: Your turn: work out the message
caption: Find the weights first. Then multiply each value by its own weight.
notes:
Can you calculate the softmax without a calculator?
Exponentiate ln 2 and zero; normalize two and one; multiply the value vectors.

title: Your turn: trace every important shape
caption: Keep patch count, embedding width and per-head width separate.
notes:
What is the difference between a patch’s 768 pixel values and the 64 embedding coordinates?
Let students write all shapes before revealing one line at a time.

title: Did we move the image, or just reorder its rows?
caption: Follow one patch and its position vector in each experiment.
notes:
Which shuffle changes what is located at the top left?
Track one patch and its position vector through each operation.

title: What else could we ask the image model to do?
caption: The output we want determines which rows we read and how we train them.
notes:
Which output would need one label, and which would need many spatial answers?
Trace CLS classification, then patch-level readouts and image–text interaction.

title: Can you talk us through the whole model?
caption: Start with the pixels. Explain what each step adds before moving to the next one.
notes:
Which step is new, and which steps did we already know?
Ask students to narrate the computation from input to loss without reading equations.
